notes: West leads the ♥K against 6♠. South wins the trick with the ♥A. South's ♥2 can go away on North's ♣K leaving South's only possible losers in the diamond suit.

If diamonds prove to be 3-3 or 4-2, South can easily take all 13 tricks. He could cash the ♣A, cross to the ♦K, discard the ♥2 on the ♣K, cash the ♦A, and cross-ruff the rest of the tricks high. As South needs only 12 tricks, he should try to guard against a 5-1 diamond break. The above line of play will fail against this distribution if West ruffs South's ♦A and returns a trump.

South should start as described, but the second round of diamonds should be ducked! East must return a trump to stop a cross-ruff. South can now ruff a low diamond, ruff back to his hand, and ruff the last low diamond. South ruffs back to his hand again. If trumps prove to be 3-2 South can draw the defenders' remaining trumps and cash the ♦A at trick 13.

The distribution of the defensive spades is only relevant when the diamonds divide 5-1. Had West followed to the second diamond, South would not need to ruff as many clubs in his hand. Notice, however, South will go down if he draws even 1 round of trump at the start of the play.

As the contract is only 6NT, South can afford to lose a club trick. South should try to guarantee taking 5 tricks from clubs.

With careful play, South can take 5 club tricks regardless of how that suit divides. After winning the diamond lead, South should cross to the North hand and lead a low club off the dummy intending to pass it if East follows small.

When East has all 5 clubs (it would have done him no good to play the ♣9), South's safety play is necessary. South can unblock the ♣A and two dummy entries still exist to establish and cash the clubs.
If, on the club lead from dummy, East discards, South rises with the ♣A. A club finesse is taken next. A club trick will be surrendered to West, but the contract will be secure.

If clubs were 3-2 or 4-1 an unnecessary trick might be lost in clubs. However, 5 club tricks will be certain as the ♣A, ♣K, and ♣Q will remove all of the defenders' remaining clubs. Notice that leading the ♣10 from dummy on the first round of the suit would be an equally effective safety play.

Trump should be drawn first. Ideally, South would like to lead hearts twice from the North hand towards South's honours. Unfortunately, both of dummy's entries must be used to finesse spades. South must lead hearts out of the closed hand.

South should start by leading a low heart, not the ♥Q or ♥J. If trumps split 2-2, South's play does not matter as only 2 heart tricks will be lost. South will have no chance if West or East has all 4 hearts.

The 3-1 trump breaks are critical. Leading low on the first round will work when either defender has a singleton honour in hearts. There are four ways this can happen. When hearts are played by leading the ♥J or ♥Q first, only two of the 3-1 breaks can be picked up (singleton ♥10 in either hand).
Starting a low trump from South, catering to four 3-1 breaks, is thus twice as likely to succeed as starting with the ♥Q or ♥J.

After winning the spade opening lead, South should start by leading a low diamond towards the South hand. East cannot afford to play the ♦A and South wins the ♦Q. South crosses back to dummy and leads another low diamond. Again East must duck and South wins the ♦J. West's discard means that South must shift his attack to the club suit.
It would be too dangerous for South to cash the top club honours. East might have started with 4 clubs to the ♣J. After winning the ♣J, East could cash the ♦A.

South can be completely sure of his contract by crossing to the dummy and leading a club to the ♣9 or ♣10. South does not care if West can win the ♣J. West has no diamonds left to return and South has 12 tricks.

If South wins the spade lead and cashes the ♣A, ♣K, and ♣Q, he will not be able to win more than 4 club tricks when clubs break 3-0. South has a certain method of guarding against this possibility.

The club suit is now unblocked. South can take 6 club tricks no matter how the suit breaks. If the defense switches at trick 3, South will eventually gain the lead. When diamonds prove to be 3-2, South will be able to reach the North hand twice in diamonds. The remaining diamond honour is played from the closed hand and overtaken by the ♦A in the dummy.

It is important not to play the ♥J on the first round of the suit. A low heart is played from the dummy, South finessing. West will win (it is actually best defense for West to duck, forcing South to guess the heart position. Luckily almost nobody could find this play). After winning his heart honour, West will clear the spades.

South can now lead the ♦2 to dummy to play hearts again. The ♥J is now played from North. East must duck and South finesses. Due to South's foresight in not playing the ♥J on the first round of the suit, the lead remains in dummy to play hearts again through East.

notes: West leads the ♠J against 5♣. It seems natural to play the ♠K or ♠Q from dummy, but there is great risk in that play. East will win the ♠A and switch to hearts. If West has the ♥K, the defense will be able to take 3 tricks (the ♣A must be knocked out before diamonds are played).

South can improve his chances by ducking in dummy at trick 1. East cannot afford to play the ♠A (that would set up 2 quick discards for South's hearts). East must duck leaving West on lead. West cannot profitably attack hearts from his side of the table. West does best to switch to a trump. If East wins the ♣A and switches to a heart, South wins the ♥A.

After drawing trump, South can set up a spade winner in dummy by taking a ruffing finesse against East's ♠A. North will have 2 winners (a spade trick and the long diamond) to take care of South's heart losers.

notes: West leads the ♥Q against 6♠. South has a potential loser in diamonds if the ♦Q is in East's hand. There is also the danger of losing a trick to the ♠K.

Looking at the trump suit in isolation, the best play is to cash the ♠A, hoping one of the defenders has a singleton ♠K. This play is slightly better than finessing in spades. The correct way to play this hand, however, involves finessing in spades. Declarer should first eliminate hearts and clubs, ruffing the third round.

South should now lead a spade towards the dummy. If West follows low, a low spade is played from North. Regardless of the position of the ♠K, the contract is secure. If West has the ♠K, there will be no trump loser. South doesn't mind losing to the ♠K in East's hand because East will be endplayed.

A heart or a club return will provide a ruff and discard taking care of South's diamond loser. A diamond return into North's tenace will be equally fatal. If West shows out when a spade is played, the ♠A is played from North. East is put on lead with the ♠K and again he is endplayed.

notes: West leads the ♥K against 3♠. The defense plays 3 rounds of hearts. South must ruff the third round of hearts small. As East has played the ♥A and ♥J, West must have all of the remaining 15 high card points for his 1NT opening.

West must have the guarded ♦K giving South a certain diamond loser. South must, therefore, avoid losing 2 trump tricks. West is known to have the ♠K and ♠J making this task more difficult. There are three trump positions that South can play for.

First, West could have doubleton ♠KJ. In that case, South can play trumps for 1 loser by ducking the first or second round of trumps completely. Second, West could have 4 spades missing the ♠10. In that case, South can hold his trump losers to 1 by playing the ♠Q through West.

The best play in the trump suit, however, is known as an intra-finesse. This play will succeed when West has 3 spades including the ♠K, the ♠J, and either the ♠5 or ♠4. Since there are two cases in which the intra-finesse works, it is superior to the other two plays. The other two plays each cater only to one case.

South should cross to the ♣K and lead a low spade. If East plays the ♠10, South covers and West wins the ♠K. South can later finesse against the ♠J. If East instead follows low, South plays low and West wins the ♠J. South can later lead the ♠Q, picking up West's ♠K and pinning East's ♠10.
After drawing trumps South can concede a trick to the West's ♦K.

If diamonds are 3-2, South can take all 13 tricks. If diamonds are 4-1, South can guarantee at least 12 tricks by finessing the ♦10 on the first round of the suit.

notes: West leads the ♠K against 6♦. There is nothing to be gained by ducking this trick, particularly since West is very likely to have 6 spades for his weak 2 opening. Dummy's ♠A wins the first trick.
Dummy has 2 extra winners that can take care of South's 2 spade losers. Unfortunately, the dummy's only entry, the ♠A, was driven out by West's opening lead.

South must enlist the defenders' help in reaching dummy's stranded winners. South should play a trump to hand noting that both defenders follow. There is only one trump outstanding which South could draw with his remaining high diamond. If South draws trump, however, he will have no possible way to get rid of his spade losers.
South should leave the last trump outstanding and cash his outside winners in hearts and clubs. South now exits with a low diamond, giving up an unnecessary trump trick.

This strange looking play is rewarded when East turns up with the outstanding trump. East has no more spades and is forced to give dummy the lead in hearts or clubs. South uses dummy's 2 winners to discard his spades losers.
If it turns out that West has the second trump (unlikely in view of West's known spade length), the contract will be down an extra trick. This is a risk worth taking for the chance of making a slam.

The correct play on this deal would have been much easier to see if East had started with all 3 diamonds. On that layout South always has a trump loser making it far easier to surrender a trump trick (after cashing South's winners in hearts, diamonds, and clubs). It is much harder when East has only 2 diamonds and South has to intentionally lose an unnecessary trump trick to succeed.

notes: West leads the ♠K against 6♥. West wins the opening spade lead and continues the suit, South ruffing. Dummy's diamond suit should eventually provide a discard for South's possible club loser, but the blockage in hearts could be a problem if trumps are 3-1.

If South cashes dummy's ♥A and ♥K and one of the defenders has a trump left, South will have no quick way back to his hand to draw the last trump. South can avoid this problem by finessing clubs at trick 3. If the club finesse wins, South can cash dummy's top trumps, cash the ♣A, and ruff a club. South is in his hand to draw the last trump.

Since the club finesse is a 50% chance and a 2-2 trump break is only about 40%, it would appear that it is best to take an immediate club finesse. However, the line of play involving drawing trump has an extra chance that makes it superior to playing on clubs.

If the ♥A and ♥K do not draw all of the outstanding trumps, South can still succeed if the defender with heart length also has 3 or more diamonds. South cashes dummy's top diamonds and when the defense is unable to ruff, South can ruff a diamond, draw trump, and claim (South's club loser goes on dummy's remaining diamond).

notes: West leads the ♥K against 3NT. South has 8 top tricks, 2 spades, the ♥A, the ♦A, and 4 clubs. The ninth trick will have to come from spades. As a diamond shift would be most unwelcome, South should win the ♥A at trick 1.

If spades are 3-3 it will be easy to establish a third spade trick. The correct play gives South an excellent chance to take 3 spade tricks when East has 4 or more spades to the ♠Q and ♠J. The club suit must provide the necessary transportation to the dummy for spade plays. South should begin by cashing the ♣A and overtaking the ♣J or ♣10 in dummy.

When clubs are 3-2, there are enough entries to play spades to best advantage. A small spade is played from dummy. If East plays low, South will win the ♠10. East must therefore split his honors. South wins the ♠K and overtakes his remaining club honor in dummy. A low spade is played towards the ♠10. East wins, blocking the suit, and plays a diamond.
After winning the ♦A, South unblocks the ♠10. South plays his ♣2 to dummy, gaining access to the ♠A.

If clubs are 4-1, South does not have enough dummy entries to pick up long spades with East headed by the ♠Q and ♠J. If West has 4 clubs, there is a reasonable chance he has a singleton spade honor. South should cash the ♠A. If West follows with an honor, South should finesse the ♠10 on the next round.

notes: West leads the ♦Q against 3NT. There are 7 top tricks, the ♠A, 2 hearts, 2 diamonds, and 2 clubs. Spades, hearts, and clubs all have potential to provide the 2 additional tricks that South needs.
As the defense is threatening to establish and run the diamonds, South would ideally like to test various suits without losing the lead.

After winning West's diamond opening lead, South should begin by cashing the ♣A and ♣K. If both opponents follow, South can surrender a club trick thereby establishing the 2 extra tricks that are needed.
When clubs are 4-1, South tries hearts next, cashing the ♥A and ♥K. If the ♥J or ♥Q appear, South can give up a heart trick. Dummy will have 2 extra heart winners and the ♠A as an entry.

When nothing good happens in hearts, South must turn his attention to spades. In order to guard against East holding 4 or more spades to the ♠K, South should lead a low spade toward his hand. If South wins this trick, he can cross to the ♠A in order to lead spades down again.
Notice that if South had tested hearts before clubs, he would have ended up in the closed hand. He would then deny himself the entries to lead spades twice toward his hand.

notes: West leads the ♣10 against 6NT. South has 9 top tricks, 3 spades, 2 hearts, the ♦A, and 3 clubs. If South can play diamonds for 1 loser he will have enough tricks for his contract.

After winning West's club opening lead, suppose South begins by cashing the ♦A and leading dummy's small diamond. East follows small. It is correct to play the ♦Q. If diamonds are 3-3 the ♦Q and ♦10 are equally likely to work. If diamonds are 4-2, however, the only 4-2 break that can be picked up is West holding the ♦J doubleton.
Although the ♦Q after the ♦A is better than a lower diamond, it still is not the proper way to play the suit.

The correct way to play diamonds is not intuitive. South should start by leading the ♦Q. When diamonds are 3-3 this play is just as good as cashing the ♦A and playing low to the ♦Q. One line will succeed when West has the ♦K third (with or without the ♦J). The other line will succeed when East has the same holdings.

When diamonds are 4-2, however, leading the ♦Q is better. Leading the ♦Q picks up the doubleton ♦K with West. Cashing the ♦A first will not pick up that holding. On all other 4-2 breaks both lines of play work equally well.
The ♦Q play loses in 1 case that cashing the ♦A succeeds. That is when there is a singleton ♦K with East. That layout, however, is much less likely than West holding the ♦K doubleton.

notes: West leads the ♣10 against 6NT. There are 11 top tricks, the ♠A, 2 hearts, 4 diamonds, and 4 clubs. Either a 3-3 heart break or a successful spade finesse will see South home. South should aim to succeed if either major suit lies favorably.

After winning West's club opening lead, if South tries spades first and the finesse loses it will be too late to play on hearts. South should therefore play on hearts first. South's plan should be to duck an early heart trick. After regaining the lead, South can test hearts and fall back on the spade finesse if hearts do not break.

It is important to try to duck the heart trick to East. If West was to gain the lead in hearts, he would return a spade, forcing South to decide on whether or not to finesse in spades before testing hearts. Proper avoidance technique involves utilizing dummy's ♥9 in the attempt to keep West off lead.

South should begin by leading a small heart toward the dummy. If West follows small, the ♥9 is played, forcing East to win the trick. If West produces a heart higher than the ♥9, dummy must win the trick. South then crosses back to his hand (with anything but the ♦10) for a second heart play.

If West is able to produce another heart higher than the ♥9, South will have to guess how to proceed. When West follows small, however, the ♥9 is played and East wins. After regaining the lead, South can cross to the ♦J (with the preserved ♦10 ), test hearts, and later take the spade finesse if hearts are 4-2.
